rationale: This full-text study is an institutional case study of Cape Verde's water and wastewater sector paired with a normative regulatory design proposal. The central mechanism analyzed is regulatory_model_ownership: the structure and mandate of Cape Verde's independent multi-sector Economic Regulation Agency (ARE, created by Law No. 20/2003), the partial privatization and subsequent re-nationalization of the main utility ELECTRA alongside municipal public utilities, and a proposed sunshine-regulation / yardstick-competition benchmarking model. Secondary mechanisms discussed include increasing-block tariffs, cross-subsidies, and proposed social tariffs (fees_tariffs_subsidies), regulatory compliance monitoring and sanctions (enforcement_sanctions), citizen participation / Water Watch Groups (participation_assistance), and complaint/appeal mechanisms (review_redress), but regulatory_model_ownership clearly dominates. On outcomes, both the descriptive sector diagnosis and the proposed regulatory KPI framework co-equally address service continuity, drinking water potability, and per-capita supply (effective_access), water and sewerage network coverage (primary_connection), tariff affordability (economic_access), and utility operational/complaint/governance metrics (administrative_outcome), justifying effective_access as primary_outcome_family and multiple for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple. The study relies on documentary legal/regulatory analysis, descriptive secondary utility/national statistics, and an illustrative benchmarking framework rather than statistical inference or primary fieldwork, best fitting qualitative (institutional case study and policy analysis).
